purpose: Make interaction part of the physical first-person world. Screens, controls, levers, tools, terminals, instruments, doors, and vehicle interfaces are objects in space with condition, power, access, and consequences.
governingPrinciple: The world is the interface. A control is an object with a location, mechanism, state, authority, and failure modes—not a floating menu pretending to be one.

controlPrinciples: Buttons have travel, force, debounce or mechanical behavior appropriate to their model.
Levers have a meaningful axis, range, detents or continuous position, resistance, and mechanical limits.
Screens expose information only when powered, connected, intact, readable, and authorized; stale or corrupted data remains visibly distinguishable.
Controls may fail, jam, be severed, lose power, become wet, overheat, or report a fault.
A valid input may be ignored or blocked by a safety interlock; feedback explains the physical or procedural reason when the character can know it.
The player's hand, tool, weapon, body, and vehicle occupy world space; interaction must respect occlusion and reach.
VR hand tracking, tracked controllers, and desktop input map to the same semantic action and object state.

informationRules: Information has source, timestamp, confidence, and access level where relevant.
A display may be incomplete because its sensor, data feed, power, or operator is impaired.
No floating omniscient HUD by default; contextual overlays are optional presentation aids, not substitutes for world instrumentation.
Important operations should have readable physical alternatives or well-designed assistive equivalents where practical.
Text size, contrast, audio/haptic cues, and reach options may adapt for accessibility without changing simulation results.
inWorldFeedback: smoke/heat/sparks when justified by simulated damage

resolutionRules: Damage follows the hit location, construction, shielding, current condition, and energy transfer model; it is not a universal 'shoot once and break' rule.
A projectile may penetrate, glance, damage a display face without disabling its controller, or damage hidden wiring behind it depending on modeled conditions.
A damaged control can fail open, fail closed, stick, misreport, or become intermittent only when supported by its modeled mechanism.
The world object persists after damage; broken controls create diagnostic, isolation, repair, replacement, and acceptance work.
Destruction does not imply the entire connected system is destroyed; dependencies and redundancy determine downstream effects.

validationGates: The same in-world object identity is used in desktop and VR views.
A visible control has a defined interaction volume and state transition.
A button or lever cannot silently bypass authority, interlocks, or physical constraints.
Damaged controls create plausible symptoms and repair work.
Screens distinguish current, stale, missing, and suspect data.
Shooting a screen does not automatically destroy unrelated connected systems.
Action and damage histories preserve provenance and consequences.
Assistive UI does not grant knowledge the character does not have.
